Pythagorean numerology alphabet chart: the quick answer

In the Pythagorean system, letters repeat through the numbers 1 to 9. A is 1, B is 2, and so on until I is 9. J starts again at 1. This simple pattern lets you convert a name into a number. The chart below is a reference for the calculation, not a scientific measure of personality or future events.

  • 1: A, J, S
  • 2: B, K, T
  • 3: C, L, U
  • 4: D, M, V
  • 5: E, N, W
  • 6: F, O, X
  • 7: G, P, Y
  • 8: H, Q, Z
  • 9: I, R

If you only need a result, try the free NumGuru calculator. If you want to understand the method, the steps below show exactly what the calculator is doing.

How to calculate a name number

Write the name you want to analyze and remove punctuation and spaces. Convert each letter with the chart, add the values, then reduce the total by adding its digits. For example, the name MAYA becomes M = 4, A = 1, Y = 7 and A = 1. The total is 13. Add 1 + 3 to get 4. In a basic Pythagorean name calculation, MAYA therefore reduces to 4.

Keep the original total as well as the reduced number. A total of 13 and a total of 31 both reduce to 4, but some numerology traditions discuss the intermediate total separately. NumGuru's core explanation uses the reduced number for a clear starting point. Different practitioners may apply additional rules, so state which method you are using when you compare results.

Step 1: choose the name consistently

For a full-name reading, use the complete name you intend to analyze, including every letter in each name. Some traditions use a birth name and others consider a current or chosen name. Neither choice changes the letter chart; it changes which letters you add. A nickname may produce a different total because it is literally a different sequence of letters.

If a name contains a hyphen or an apostrophe, ignore the punctuation and keep the letters. For names written in another alphabet, transliteration can change the result. Choose one spelling, record it, and avoid comparing totals produced from different spellings as though they were the same input.

Step 2: turn each letter into a number

Read the chart row by row, or use the repeating A-to-I pattern. For a longer worked example, the name LUNA gives L = 3, U = 3, N = 5 and A = 1. The sum is 12, and 1 + 2 = 3. You can check the arithmetic yourself: 3 + 3 + 5 + 1 = 12. Writing down each letter value is the easiest way to catch a skipped or duplicated letter.

Step 3: reduce the total

When the total has more than one digit, add the digits and repeat until you have one digit. A total of 29 becomes 2 + 9 = 11, then 1 + 1 = 2 under a simple one-digit method. Some Pythagorean readers retain 11, 22 or 33 as master numbers instead of reducing them immediately. That is a convention within numerology, not a mathematical necessity. If your result is one of those totals, show both the total and its reduced value so readers can understand the choice.

What does the result mean?

The letter-to-number chart answers a calculation question. Interpretation is a separate step. Numerology readers often use a full-name total as an Expression or Destiny number and use other parts of a name for other core numbers. A vowel-only calculation is commonly called a Soul Urge number, while a consonant-only calculation is commonly called a Personality number. These names describe a traditional framework for self-reflection; they are not diagnostic categories.

For example, a reduced 4 is often associated in Pythagorean interpretations with structure, routine and steady work. That association is a theme for reflection, not a promise that a person will have a particular career or outcome. A useful reading asks whether the theme resonates with lived experience instead of treating the number as proof.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Mixing charts: Chaldean and Pythagorean systems assign different values. Use the chart shown here throughout a single calculation.
  • Skipping letters: Include every letter in the chosen spelling, even repeated letters.
  • Changing the input midway: A birth name and a current name are different inputs; label them separately.
  • Hiding the arithmetic: Show both the unreduced total and the final reduction, especially when 11, 22 or 33 appears.
  • Overstating meaning: Numerology is an interpretive practice, so avoid presenting a number as a verified forecast.

Try your own example

Pick a short name, list each letter and look it up in the nine-row chart. Add the values once, then check the sum independently. If you want to explore a fuller report, compare the name result with the birth-date calculation and learn how the different numbers are defined in NumGuru's method guide. You can also use the free calculator to compare your hand calculation with the site's result. Keep the spelling and calculation method consistent, and treat any interpretation as a prompt for curiosity rather than a fixed verdict.
